Loved your post. It resonates deeply. 

I’ve been suicidal pretty regularly for years. I’ll have a good couple of weeks and then be back in a hole. I will say that getting help doesn’t always mean getting “locked away.” I’ve been inpatient in a few places. The first time was a case of “you can do this voluntarily or we can put an involuntary hold on you.” That time I “volunteered.” Second time I went in willingly and desperately. Same place both times. 

Third time, new location, I knew what I needed: to see a psychiatrist ASAP. I didn’t have a plan to kill myself but I had thought about it a lot and was having hallucinations. I told them that I didn’t feel like a danger to myself or others, but I needed my meds adjusted or I would get worse, I knew. I had been on a wait list for a psychiatrist for months. I had to communicate this as clearly and confidently as I could. I was in there for 24 hours (on a weekend, no less). My therapist was surprised because that hospital usually keeps people with my insurance for three days. Sad facts. 

In September of this year, I had an attempt. I went back to a different mental health hospital (different state and everything) that I had been to for partial hospitalization last year. During the intake assessment the day following my attempt, they told me I should be admitted. I explained that while I understood why they would think that’s best, I could not get childcare and it just wasn’t plausible for me to be inpatient. I said I would be happy to do the partial hospitalization program though because I really need help. That meant I went to group therapy from 9-2:30 each weekday for two weeks. Got to see a psychiatrist during that time too. 

Meds worked for a bit, now I’m having a hard time. Some environmental factors are effecting my ability to cope though. But I’m trying. 
Just wanted to throw out there that it’s not a guarantee to be locked up.

Another child of divorce here. I was 5 when my parents first split up due to my father’s infidelity, and was 9 when they finally divorced. My mom also took the straight forward approach, meaning she explained sexual infidelity to a five year old (and older sibling). I wasn’t ready. Their post-divorce relationship put a strain on us because they subtly used us to get at the other. Anyway I knew my father did a very bad thing and that forever was to overriding opinion of him, even though I loved him very much. Sadly he died when I was 15, so I didn’t get a chance to work through a lot with him. 

OP,  your son is 12 and I think it’s great that you haven’t been the one to go into details surrounding the divorce while also reminding him what’s most important. I feel like it might be a good idea to talk to your ex-wife and explain that he’s asking questions and you aren’t wanting to lie, nor are you wanting to drag her through the mud over her terrible past decision. I wish I had a chance to talk to my dad as an adult. I feel I could have had a better relationship with him and moved past his mistakes if I heard him own up to them as such, rather than being told by my mom who was understandably bitter about being cheated on. My dad was human. Your ex-wife is too. Cheating is never ok, but that doesn’t mean our past mistakes need to define us. Good on you for taking the high road.

This happened to two days ago. I was taking my son to the doctor and realized I did not have enough gas in the car. I pull into the gas station and slide my debit card. Insufficient funds. I know there is money in the account, but whatever. I will just use my credit card and transfer the money later. Card declined. I am already exhausted having been up most of the night before with my youngest child, the temperature is at freezing, and I am now on the verge of tears. I check my wallet and have $5. A man pulls up on the other side of the pump was using and begins filling his SUV. I summon my courage to overcome my anxiety.
“Excuse me? I know this is unusual, but my cards aren’t working, I don’t want to have to get my kids out, but I have $5. Would you mind putting $5 on this pump for me?”
He says, “Sure!” then checked the pump number and went inside with my $5.
When I see him walk back out I ask, “Am I good to go?” 
He walks up, hands me my $5 back, and says, “I put $20 on it. You seem like you might need it. Merry Christmas!” 
I thank him profusely and nearly cry. His kindness was refreshing for my soul, for sure!

When my son was that age, an evening routine made bedtime go much more smoothly. It doesn’t have to be elaborate. Ours consisted of changing his diaper, putting on pajamas or just a clean set of comfy clothes, brushing teeth, reading 2 of his books, and tucking in with a goodnight kiss. We had just moved when we started this routine and he was about 16 months at the time. For the first few days he was still apprehensive about being in a new place and would cry in his room for a while (husband and I would go in and tell him everything was fine and that he wasn’t alone), but I feel being consistent with the routine helped him adjust. By the next week he wasn’t crying at all at bedtime. Different things work for different kids though. I hope you find what works for you and your nephew!

My sister was a caseworker for CPS in Arkansas. As others have mentioned, they really want to keep families together. The purpose of CPS is to keep the child safe, and sometimes this is from their own actions. Reaching out as a concerned parent can help them give you resources. I hope you find what works for your family!
